title: Romario Renews Call for Ancelotti to Leave Brazil After Japan Defeat
deck: The Brazil great has twice urged the national team to change course after a 3-2 friendly loss to Japan, while Ancelotti insists he is entitled to face criticism.
author: Ayush Sharma
label: International football
seoTitle: Romario Calls for Ancelotti Exit After Brazil Defeat
metaDescription: Romario has renewed his demand for Carlo Ancelotti to leave Brazil after the 3-2 loss to Japan, despite a subsequent 7-0 win over Singapore.
imageAlt: Mr Anfield Football editorial stadium banner

facts.label: Brazil's friendly defeat to Japan

body.text: Carlo Ancelotti's Brazil project has been pulled into another public argument after Romario renewed his demand for the Italian to leave the national-team job. The former striker has criticised the coach twice in the space of a week, turning a difficult run of results into a debate about the direction of the Seleção ahead of the next major tournament.

The dispute intensified after Brazil lost 3-2 to Japan in a friendly. Tatsuhiro Sakamoto scored a late winner, while Ancelotti was sent off for dissent in the aftermath. Barcelona forward Raphinha also saw red. Romario used the defeat to question what the former Real Madrid manager had added to the national team and argued that Brazil should not spend another cycle waiting for a new identity to emerge.

Ancelotti has defended the right of former players to express their opinions and indicated that the team remains part of a developing project. Romario repeated his position before another Brazil fixture, insisting his own history with the national team gives him a voice in the conversation. The exchange has become about more than one friendly defeat: it is a public disagreement over patience, identity and expectations.

Brazil's emphatic 7-0 victory over Singapore, featuring a hat-trick from Vinícius Júnior, offered a more positive answer on the pitch. It does not automatically settle the larger questions. A friendly win can restore confidence, but the pressure on Ancelotti will ultimately be judged by performances against stronger opponents and by whether Brazil look more coherent when the margins are tighter.

Ancelotti arrived with a remarkable club record and a reputation for managing elite dressing rooms, but international management leaves less time to train and build patterns. Romario wants a visible change now; Ancelotti needs to show that the project is progressing. The result against Singapore helps, yet the debate is unlikely to disappear after one good night.

title: Piqué Defends Jesús Owono After 12-Match Ban Following Fatal Collision
deck: The FC Andorra owner says the punishment should judge the challenge itself rather than the tragic outcome, while Tenerife's manager disagrees.
author: Ayush Sharma
label: Football news
metaDescription: Gerard Piqué has questioned Jesús Owono's 12-match suspension after the collision that preceded Jesús de Miguel's death. FC Andorra will not appeal.
imageAlt: Mr Anfield Football editorial stadium banner

facts.label: Suspension imposed on Jesús Owono
Date of the Tenerife v FC Andorra collision
When Jesús de Miguel died in hospital
FC Andorra's decision on the ban

body.text: Gerard Piqué has publicly defended FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono after the Spanish football authorities handed him a 12-match suspension following the collision that preceded the death of Tenerife forward Jesús de Miguel. Piqué, the club's majority shareholder, argues that the disciplinary process must assess the action on the pitch rather than allow the terrible consequence to determine the punishment.

The incident happened on November 2 during a Spanish second-division match. Owono came out to challenge for a ball and collided with De Miguel, who was taken to hospital and died the following day. The Spanish federation's disciplinary committee imposed the maximum sanction for the serious offence it identified, relying on the referee's description of a forceful challenge while the ball was in play.

Piqué questioned whether the same disciplinary standard would have been applied had the collision not ended in a fatality. He compared the case with another recent Spanish incident in which a player received a shorter suspension after accidentally kicking an opponent in the head. His argument is that the action and the outcome should not be treated as interchangeable when deciding a sporting penalty.

FC Andorra general manager Jaume Nogués has said the club will not appeal. He indicated that an appeal would be socially difficult and that Owono himself was not in favour of challenging the decision. Nogués nevertheless criticised the way the case had been handled. Tenerife manager Álvaro Cervera rejected Piqué's interpretation, saying he believed the challenge could have been avoided.

The human loss must remain at the centre of the story. De Miguel's death has affected both clubs and the wider football community, while Owono is also dealing with the emotional consequences of the incident. A suspension cannot resolve that grief. The disciplinary decision, the club's decision not to appeal and the different views about responsibility can be reported clearly without reducing a tragedy to a football argument.

title: Jorge Jesus Responds to Ronaldo's Mother After Portugal Tribute Row

label: International football

imageAlt: Mr Anfield Football editorial stadium banner

facts.label: Date Ronaldo announced his international retirement

body.text: Portugal coach Jorge Jesus has been drawn into another public discussion about Cristiano Ronaldo after the forward's mother criticised the way her son's international career came to an end. Dolores Aveiro said Ronaldo had been deceived and questioned why the national team's tribute was staged after his retirement rather than in his presence. Jesus responded by saying he respects her, while making clear that he is frustrated by the repeated questions.

Ronaldo announced his international retirement on November 5, bringing an end to a Portugal career that included 234 appearances and 146 goals. Portugal marked his absence before the 4-1 defeat to Denmark by having the players wear his famous No. 7 shirt before kick-off. The gesture was intended as recognition of a player whose influence on the national team stretched across generations.

Aveiro's reaction was more complicated. She was unhappy with the way the farewell had been handled and said she was glad to see Portugal lose to Denmark. Her comments added to an already sensitive debate following Ronaldo's departure and the circumstances around his final period with the national team.

Jesus was asked about the remarks ahead of Portugal's Nations League meeting with Wales. He questioned why he was expected to answer for a player's mother, but also described Aveiro as a woman he respects and acknowledged the sacrifices she made raising her family. His response was defensive rather than dismissive: he did not attempt to turn the disagreement into a personal attack.

The story now sits between two separate issues: the way Portugal honoured Ronaldo and the reasons the striker chose to retire. A pre-match tribute can recognise a career, but it cannot replace a farewell in front of supporters or resolve a disagreement about how the final chapter unfolded. With Jesus saying the subject may continue into next year, Portugal's focus will have to return to the team rather than the noise surrounding one of its greatest players.

body.text: Mauricio Pochettino has given Pep Guardiola a direct recommendation as the United States searches for its next men's national-team coach: take the job. Pochettino, who is leaving the USMNT to become Manchester United head coach, believes the role is now more attractive to leading European coaches than it was before the 2026 World Cup.

Pochettino described the moment as an ideal time to arrive at the federation. He pointed to the direction of the programme, the quality of the player pool and the new National Training Centre. His argument is that the job should no longer be viewed as a step away from elite club football, but as an ambitious international project with resources and talent capable of supporting a clear playing identity.

The United States are also coming off a World Cup on home soil in which they reached the round of 16. Pochettino's time in charge has included work to improve the team's intensity and identify younger players who can become important parts of the national setup. The next coach will inherit a programme with a stronger profile, but also the responsibility to turn that attention into consistent results.

Guardiola is an obvious name to attract attention because of his record at Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Manchester City. He has stepped away from club management after a decade at City and is understood to be taking a sabbatical. There has been speculation about the US vacancy, but no formal agreement with Guardiola should be assumed from Pochettino's public endorsement.

Pochettino has also spoken about missing the daily rhythm of club management: training every day, preparing for a match each weekend and working closely with players. Manchester United offers that routine again, while the US job offered a different challenge between international windows. His advice to Guardiola is an endorsement of the project, not confirmation that the Spaniard will accept it.

title: Pochettino Cannot Fix Manchester United Alone: The Owners Face Their Own Test
deck: The new head coach inherits the first team, but the club's repeated changes of direction raise a bigger question about accountability across the Glazer and INEOS structure.
author: Ayush Sharma
label: Manchester United analysis
seoTitle: Pochettino Cannot Fix Manchester United Alone
metaDescription: Mauricio Pochettino inherits Manchester United's crisis, but the Glazers, Jim Ratcliffe and the football leadership must provide a stable plan.
imageAlt: Mr Anfield Football editorial stadium banner

facts.label: Manchester United's league position when Pochettino took the job
United's league victories after the opening 10 matches
Key layers of ownership and football leadership under scrutiny
Pochettino's scheduled first match against Liverpool

body.text: Mauricio Pochettino has arrived at Manchester United with a familiar challenge: restore confidence, improve performances and make a talented but uneven squad look like a coherent team. Yet the manager cannot solve the club's deeper problems on his own. United's repeated changes of direction have raised questions about who defines the football strategy, who is responsible for recruitment and who is ultimately held accountable when the plan fails.

The ownership structure makes those questions difficult to avoid. The Glazer family remain majority owners, while Jim Ratcliffe and INEOS have taken responsibility for football operations following their minority investment. Chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox are also central to the sporting structure. That may be a workable division of responsibilities, but it requires clear authority and a shared long-term plan.

United's recent managerial history illustrates the cost of inconsistency. Coaches with very different ideas have followed one another, and recruitment has often left the next manager trying to make players signed for another system fit his own. A new appointment can create an immediate lift, but it cannot by itself fix scouting, squad planning, player development, medical availability or decision-making above the dressing room.

Pochettino's strengths are clear: demanding training, aggressive pressing, strong man-management and a track record of improving younger players. Those qualities can help a team quickly. But the club must decide what it wants to be beyond his preferred formation. If the recruitment strategy changes every time a manager leaves, the same cycle will repeat, no matter how respected the next coach may be.

The first months will therefore test more than Pochettino's tactical ability. United's leadership must give him a clear remit, build a recruitment process that supports a consistent football identity and accept responsibility for decisions that sit outside the head coach's control. The Glazers, Ratcliffe, Berrada and Wilcox will be judged by whether they create that structure. The manager can lead the team; the owners and executives have to make sure the club is finally built to support him.

title: Pochettino's Manchester United To-Do List: Fix the Defence Before Chasing a New Identity
deck: United have been too easy to play through, too generous with high-quality chances and too inconsistent in the final third. The new manager has several problems to solve.
author: Ayush Sharma
label: Tactical analysis
metaDescription: Mauricio Pochettino inherits a Manchester United side with major defensive and structural problems. Here are the priorities for his rebuild.
imageAlt: Mr Anfield Football editorial stadium banner

facts.label: United's position in the table before Pochettino's arrival
Expected goals conceded per opponent shot
Opposition shots taken from inside the box
Set-piece goals conceded

body.text: Mauricio Pochettino does not inherit a Manchester United side that needs only a change of mood. The numbers point to structural problems at both ends of the pitch. United have struggled to control the quality of chances they concede, while their own possession has not consistently translated into clear opportunities. The new manager's first job is to make the team harder to play against before trying to impose a complete new identity.

The most alarming defensive figure is the quality of opposition shots. United have been allowing around 0.19 expected goals per shot, the highest rate in the Premier League at the time of the analysis. More than 74 per cent of opponents' attempts have come from inside the penalty area. That suggests the issue is not simply that rivals are shooting often; they are getting into dangerous locations and finding space to finish.

United have also looked caught between styles. They can keep the ball and progress it through midfield, but the press has not consistently forced turnovers high up the pitch. When possession breaks down, the defensive structure can be exposed in transition. In attack, the team can generate a high volume of attempts without producing the same level of high-quality chances. The balance between patient build-up, pressure after losing the ball and direct counter-attacks has not been clear.

Pochettino's pressing approach could help, but intensity alone is not a plan. The distances between the front line, midfield and defence have to be coordinated. The full-backs need clear roles, the midfield must protect the central spaces and the centre-backs need support when the first press is bypassed. United also need more reliable set-piece work after conceding six goals from dead-ball situations while scoring only once in the league at that stage.

Recruitment and development are just as important. The squad has been assembled across several managerial eras, leaving a mixture of profiles and players who have struggled to stay fit or find a role. Pochettino has a history of improving young players, and that may be a route to progress with Kobbie Mainoo, Leny Yoro and other academy prospects. But the club must support him with consistent decisions. A clear system, a healthier squad and better chance control would be more meaningful first steps than another headline transfer.

title: Klopp's Germany Crush the Netherlands 5-0 to Storm Into Nations League Last Eight
deck: A disciplined first half gave way to a ruthless second-half burst as Germany scored four times after the break and claimed top spot in Group A2.
author: Ayush Sharma
label: Match analysis
metaDescription: Germany hammered the Netherlands 5-0 under Jürgen Klopp, with Florian Wirtz scoring twice as the hosts sealed top spot in Nations League Group A2.
imageAlt: Mr Anfield Football editorial stadium banner

facts.label: Germany's final score against the Netherlands
Derry Scherhant's opening goal
Florian Wirtz goals
Germany goals after half-time

body.text: Jürgen Klopp's Germany delivered their most emphatic statement yet with a 5-0 Nations League victory over the Netherlands in Berlin. The scoreline was decisive, but the performance was also a lesson in patience. Germany did not force risky passes simply to prove they could play through the Dutch press. They kept their approach direct when needed, waited for spaces to open and then punished the visitors in a devastating second half.

Derry Scherhant put Germany ahead in the 41st minute after the hosts had survived a warning when Donyell Malen missed a good opportunity. The goal gave Klopp's side something to protect at the break, but it also changed the tempo of the contest. Germany returned with greater confidence and began finding the spaces behind the Dutch midfield more regularly.

Florian Wirtz doubled the lead shortly after the hour, and Nico Schlotterbeck made it three with a header from a Brajan Gruda delivery. Wirtz scored again in the 71st minute before Gruda added the fifth six minutes later. Four goals in a short spell turned a competitive group decider into a rout and gave the home supporters a performance to remember.

Klopp later explained that Germany had simplified parts of their build-up because the team had only a limited time to rehearse the patterns. With both sides looking to press high, the match could easily have become a contest of rushed short passes and turnovers. Germany were prepared to play beyond that pressure and accelerate when a passing lane appeared. The decision reduced unnecessary risk and allowed their attacking quality to decide the game.

The result sends Germany through as Group A2 winners, with the Netherlands also reaching the quarter-finals. For Klopp, the bigger gain is the sense that the team can adapt rather than follow one rigid route. The performance does not guarantee success in the knockout rounds, where opponents will bring different problems, but Germany now have a clear example of how disciplined decision-making can unlock their attacking talent.

body.text: Andoni Iraola has given Liverpool supporters a glimpse of life away from the training ground after taking time to watch a children's grassroots football match in Maghull. A photograph shared by Maghull FC, showing the Liverpool head coach with young players, quickly spread across social media and attracted around one million views.

The visit appears to have been a personal one rather than a planned club event. Maghull manager Joe Burns told BBC Radio Merseyside that Iraola had gone to watch a relative and was approached by children who recognised him. Burns said the coach spent time taking photographs with the youngsters and did not rush away, leaving families delighted by the unexpected encounter.

That reaction matters in a city where football is part of everyday life. Premier League managers operate under constant pressure, with their weeks shaped by training schedules, media duties and results. A visit to a junior match is a small gesture, but for children who follow the game closely, meeting a top-level coach can become a lasting memory.

The episode also fits a broader truth about football clubs: their connection with a community is not built only through results at Anfield. Grassroots teams provide the first experience of the sport for thousands of children, and local pitches depend on volunteers, coaches and parents. When a high-profile figure takes an interest in that level of the game, it sends a positive message without needing a commercial campaign.

Iraola's visit should not be exaggerated into a statement about tactics or transfer plans. It was simply a human moment that resonated because it felt spontaneous. The response from Maghull's players and families shows why these interactions matter, and why the best football stories are sometimes found far below the bright lights of the Premier League.

title: Andy Robertson Surpasses Kenny Dalglish to Become Scotland's Most-Capped Player
deck: The Liverpool defender reached 103 appearances against Switzerland, breaking a record held by Dalglish for four decades on a difficult night for Scotland.
author: Ayush Sharma
label: International football
seoTitle: Andy Robertson Breaks Scotland Caps Record
metaDescription: Andy Robertson earned his 103rd Scotland cap against Switzerland, moving beyond Kenny Dalglish's long-standing record of 102 appearances.
imageAlt: Mr Anfield Football editorial stadium banner

facts.label: Robertson's Scotland appearances
Dalglish's previous record
Time Dalglish's record had stood
Scotland's defeat to Switzerland

body.text: Andy Robertson has become Scotland's most-capped men's international after making his 103rd appearance in the 4-0 Nations League defeat to Switzerland. The milestone moved the defender beyond Kenny Dalglish, whose record of 102 caps had stood for 40 years. It was a personal landmark of enormous significance, even though the result made the evening a difficult one for the national team.

Robertson had already drawn level with Dalglish in Scotland's previous match, a 2-1 win over North Macedonia. Starting against Switzerland gave him the record outright. Dalglish represented Scotland between 1971 and 1986, while Robertson made his debut in 2014 and has gone on to captain the side through major tournaments and multiple Nations League campaigns.

The contrast between the individual achievement and the team result was stark. Scotland began with a competitive spell but fell behind through a Lewis Ferguson own goal. Switzerland then took control after the interval, with Winsley Boteli, Alvyn Sanches and Zeki Amdouni adding to the score. The 4-0 defeat ended Scotland's hopes of reaching the Nations League play-offs and left the team facing questions about its consistency.

Robertson has always spoken with admiration for Dalglish and made clear that the former Liverpool and Celtic forward remains his benchmark. That respect is important because the record is not simply a number. Dalglish's 102 appearances were part of an era in which Scotland regularly relied on its best players to carry the team through qualification and major tournaments. Robertson's achievement reflects the longevity and leadership required to reach the same level.

For Scotland, the next challenge is to make the most of the experience Robertson brings. The defender's milestone deserves recognition, but the captain himself will be more concerned with the performance that accompanied it. A record-breaking night should be remembered as a major moment in his career; the heavy defeat is a reminder that Scotland still have work to do if they want to turn individual quality into consistent international results.

body.text: Nike is set to replace Adidas as the official match-ball supplier across UEFA's men's club competitions from the 2027-28 season, ending one of the Champions League's most recognisable commercial partnerships. The agreement runs through 2031 and covers the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League, as well as a number of associated UEFA competitions.

The deal is broader than a simple change to the ball used in Europe's leading club tournament. Nike will also supply match balls for the UEFA Super Cup, UEFA Youth League and UEFA Futsal Champions League. It is the first time the same supplier will provide the official ball for all three major men's club competitions, giving the American company a consistent presence across UEFA's club calendar.

Adidas has supplied the Champions League ball since 2001, with each season bringing a fresh design that became part of the competition's visual identity. The change will therefore be noticeable to supporters as well as players. The star-panel design and its seasonal variations have become closely associated with European nights, and Nike will have to create a look that feels new without losing the prestige of the tournament.

UEFA's commercial operation, UC3, said the agreement followed a competitive tender process. Nike described the return to the Champions League as a major opportunity and said it wanted to combine innovation with respect for the tradition of the competitions. Details of the first ball designs have not yet been released, so the immediate significance is the commercial switch rather than any confirmed change to playing characteristics.

For Nike, the deal is about visibility at the centre of elite club football. A match ball is used in every game and appears in every broadcast, giving it a different kind of exposure from a shirt sponsorship. Adidas's long association means the company will be missed from one of football's most recognisable stages, but the move also creates an opportunity for UEFA and Nike to launch a new visual era beginning in 2027.

title: Mohamed Salah's Egypt Scoring Record: Why the 70-Goal Claim Is Disputed
deck: The Egyptian FA counts Salah on 70 goals after his brace against Malawi, but FIFA's revised total is 68 and the return match ended goalless.
author: Ayush Sharma
label: International football
seoTitle: Mohamed Salah Egypt Record: 70 or 68 Goals?
metaDescription: Mohamed Salah scored twice in Egypt's 5-0 win over Malawi, but a dispute between the Egyptian FA and FIFA leaves his official record unclear.
imageAlt: Mr Anfield Football editorial stadium banner

facts.label: Egyptian FA's total for Salah
FIFA's revised total after the Malawi brace
Hossam Hassan's recognised record under FIFA's count
Egypt's first win over Malawi
Score in the return fixture on 17 November

body.text: Mohamed Salah's latest international milestone has become a statistical dispute rather than a straightforward record announcement. The Egypt forward scored twice in a 5-0 victory over Malawi on November 13, and the Egyptian Football Association credited him with 70 international goals, a total that would move him beyond Hossam Hassan. FIFA's revised count, however, places Salah on 68, leaving Hassan's recognised tally of 69 ahead.

The disagreement centres on two goals Salah scored in a 10-0 friendly win over Swaziland, now Eswatini, in 2013. Those goals appear in the Egyptian association's count but are not included in FIFA's revised total because the match did not meet the governing body's criteria for a full international. That difference has followed Salah throughout the latest milestone and explains why reports have described the same event in different ways.

The goals against Malawi were still significant. Salah scored late in the 5-0 win in Cairo, first with a header and then from the penalty spot. The result gave new coach Ali Maher a strong start and moved Egypt to the top of their qualifying group at the halfway point. The national association celebrated the achievement using its own statistical record, while FIFA's website was amended to show the lower total.

The return fixture in Lilongwe on November 17 ended 0-0, so Salah did not add to either tally. Egypt remain well placed in the group but have not yet secured qualification. The draw also means the discussion about the scoring record remains unresolved under FIFA's figures: Salah is one goal short of Hassan on the governing body's count, while the Egyptian FA's figure continues to put him in front.

It is fair to say the Egyptian FA recognises Salah as its all-time leading scorer on 70 goals. It is also accurate to say FIFA's revised figure is 68, one behind Hassan's 69. Rather than choosing one number and ignoring the other, the record should be reported with the counting difference explained. Salah's achievement is historic either way, but the official record depends on which institution's match list is being used.

body.text: Alexis Mac Allister's father has confirmed that renewal talks between the midfielder and Liverpool have not yet begun, adding uncertainty to a contract situation that could become important over the next year. Carlos Mac Allister says his son still has around 20 months remaining on his current deal and that the position is being reviewed following changes in the club's sporting leadership and coaching staff.

Mac Allister joined Liverpool from Brighton in 2023 and became a key part of the side that won the Premier League title in 2024-25. His ability to receive under pressure, progress the ball and contribute defensively has made him an important midfielder. He has continued to feature regularly under Andoni Iraola, which makes the absence of formal renewal discussions a subject worth watching rather than evidence that an exit is already planned.

Carlos said there could be news before the end of the year, but he was careful not to suggest negotiations were close. He also made clear that the family is focused on Liverpool and does not intend to use the situation to discuss other clubs. His comments were framed around respect for the team that signed his son and gave him the platform to compete at the highest level.

There are several reasons why a renewal may take time. Liverpool have changed their sporting director and manager, and a new football structure may want to assess the squad before committing to long-term contracts. Mac Allister's age, status and importance to the team will also shape any discussion. From the club's perspective, waiting too long can increase uncertainty; from the player's perspective, there is still time to understand the new direction.

For now, the most accurate description is simple: there have been no renewal talks, but Mac Allister is not being presented as a player pushing for an immediate departure. Liverpool must decide how central he is to the next version of the team, while the midfielder continues to perform. With a busy season ahead and a major fixture against Manchester United at Anfield on November 22, the focus remains on football before the contract conversation becomes urgent.

title: From Ballon d'Or Dreams to Madrid's Bench: Should Liverpool Bring Trent Back?
deck: Alexander-Arnold's move to Real Madrid has not produced the role he imagined, but a return to Anfield would carry sporting, financial and emotional complications.
author: Ayush Sharma
label: Transfer analysis
seoTitle: Should Liverpool Bring Trent Alexander-Arnold Back?
metaDescription: Trent Alexander-Arnold is struggling for starts at Real Madrid. We assess whether a Liverpool return makes sense for the player and the club.

body.text: Trent Alexander-Arnold left Liverpool with the ambition of reaching another level at Real Madrid, and his long-term dream of becoming the first full-back to win the Ballon d'Or. Eighteen months later, his move has become a difficult story. Injuries, managerial change and competition for places have limited his opportunities, creating an uncomfortable question for both player and former club: would a return to Anfield make sense?

Alexander-Arnold has started only 18 of a possible 50 LaLiga matches since joining Madrid. This season, he has featured in just five of 16 matches across competitions and has started four league games. Denzel Dumfries arrived from Inter in the summer, while Federico Valverde has also been used at right-back. The appointment of José Mourinho has added another complication, with the manager's preferences not always appearing to suit Alexander-Arnold's strongest creative qualities.

Liverpool could still benefit from what made him special. He redefined the right-back role at Anfield with his passing range, crossing and ability to create chances from deep. He left with 64 Premier League assists, a record for a defender in the competition. Liverpool's attack has lacked consistent chance creation this season, and a player capable of delivering early switches and precise balls into the box would offer a different dimension.

But nostalgia cannot be the basis of a transfer. Alexander-Arnold signed a long contract at Madrid that runs to 2031, meaning any move would require financial agreement with the Spanish club. His injury record is also a concern: muscle problems have interrupted his time in Spain, following a series of absences during his final seasons at Liverpool. The club would need to be confident that he could stay available and fit into Iraola's structure.

There is an emotional question too. Alexander-Arnold's departure was painful for many supporters because he was a homegrown player who had spent much of his life at Liverpool. A return that looked like a retreat after a difficult spell in Madrid could be complicated for him and for the fanbase. The player still has time to establish himself at Madrid, and Liverpool should not mistake a difficult start for a guaranteed exit.

The best conclusion is that a reunion is possible in theory but far from straightforward. Liverpool would gain elite distribution and a familiar connection with the club, but they would also take on wages, a transfer fee, injury risk and a complicated public narrative. Alexander-Arnold must first find a way to earn a regular role at Madrid. Only then can both sides decide whether a return is a positive football decision rather than a reaction to disappointment.
